Cyber Animism (talk hosted by Michael Levin's center, Tufts)
AGI-24 keynote on cyber animism (Seattle; Machine Learning Street Talk recording)
From Artificial Intelligence to Artificial Consciousness (TEDxBeaconStreet)
If a machine became conscious, how would we know? (TED, TEDAI Vienna)

references.name: Aristotle
references.tldr: Greek philosopher who systematised logic, physics and psychology. He described the soul (psyche) not as a ghostly substance but as the organising form of a living body, with vegetative, animal and rational layers.
references.bach_take: Bach names Aristotle as the possible start of the project of 'naturalizing the mind' that AI continues, and rereads him 'as a computer scientist': the soul is software, a causal pattern imposed on physics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Aristotle already said that the soul is a form a pattern imposed on physics I think what he meant is it's a causal pattern
Paraphrase: philosophy's 'plot' starts with Leibniz, 'maybe even with Aristotle'.
he talks about the soul or psyche as the animating principle of living matter
For Aristotle there are several layers to our soul to our psyche. The first one is the layer that plants have the vegetative layer.

references.name: Unmoved mover (first mover)
references.author: Aristotle
references.tldr: Aristotle argued that if anything in the universe changes, something must ultimately drive that change without itself being moved. This 'prime mover' is the minimal philosophical notion of a god: no personality, just the reason things keep going.
references.bach_take: Bach ranks gods by 'metaphysical cost' and calls this the cheapest, a '1st degree god', which he equates with the transition function of a computational universe.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I would say that is the primary computational transition function of the universe.
Paraphrase (German): Aristotle's first mover is the primary state transition function, the Turing machine that drives our universe.

references.name: Plato's theory of forms / Platonism
references.author: Plato
references.tldr: Plato held that behind the changing things we perceive there are ideal, timeless forms (the perfect triangle, the ideal table). In mathematics, 'Platonism' is the view that mathematical objects really exist independently of minds.
references.bach_take: In 2016 Bach calls mathematical Platonism an illusion: mathematics feels real because it 'writes itself' from axioms. In 2025 he reinterprets Plato's forms as dimensions of an embedding space, calling Plato the first to write about it.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: this notion that the metaphysics of mathematics is real is called Platonism. I think it's an illusion.
I suspect that Plato is the first guy who wrote about the embedding space that we discovered much later in AI.

references.name: Thomas Aquinas
references.tldr: Medieval theologian who merged Aristotle with Christian doctrine. He argued for God as the necessary ground of existence and described seven virtues: four practical ones (temperance, justice, prudence, courage) and three theological ones (faith, hope, love).
references.bach_take: Bach treats Aquinas's God as a 'transcendental principle' (a 2nd degree god) and later reads the virtues as rational policies for agents: the practical virtues for individuals, and faith, love and hope as policies that create a collective agent.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: This is the god of Thomas of Aquinus. The God that Thomas of Aquinus discovered is not the god of Abraham
aquinus in some sense defines God as the best possible most top level Collective agent
Paraphrase (German): the god of Thomas Aquinas is god as a transcendent principle, merely the reason why something exists rather than nothing.

references.name: Mind-body dualism (res cogitans / res extensa)
references.author: René Descartes
references.tldr: Descartes divided reality into two substances: thinking stuff (res cogitans, the mind) and extended stuff in space (res extensa, matter). The puzzle ever since is how the two could interact.
references.bach_take: Bach starts his history of mind with Descartes, then reinterprets him: both substances are real, but both are representations inside the mind, a world model and a sphere of ideas, generated by the brain.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: we very often start philosophy of mind with looking at Descartes. That is: at dualism.
Paraphrase: Descartes' res cogitans is the 'ideosphere' and res extensa the 'stuff in space', but both exist inside the mind's representations.
Descartes's dualism is actually not a dualism about substances outside of ourselves
Paraphrase: the sphere of ideas is what Descartes calls res cogitans; the world model is res extensa.

references.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
references.tldr: German polymath who co-invented calculus and dreamed of a universal symbolic language in which disputes could be settled by calculation ('let us calculate').
references.bach_take: For Bach, Leibniz is where the project of mechanising thought begins in earnest: translating thoughts into numbers and resolving arguments by computation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (name garbled as 'li Nets'): Leibniz had the idea that we can translate thoughts and arguments into numbers and resolve arguments by calculation.
Paraphrase (garbled as 'lights'): Leibniz had the insight that you need to mathematize the mind and translate it into a kind of mathematical machine.

references.notes: Name appears as 'li Nets', 'lipets', 'lights' in YouTube auto-captions; resolved from context (listed between Aristotle and La Mettrie/Frege).

references.name: Leibniz's mill argument
references.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
references.tldr: A thought experiment from the Monadology: imagine a thinking machine enlarged to the size of a mill so you can walk inside. You would see only parts pushing each other and nothing that explains perception. Leibniz concluded that mechanism cannot explain mind.
references.bach_take: Bach presents it as the classic intuition against AI and answers that the modern notion of computation, not cogs and levers, is the right picture of a machine.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And what you are going to see is just parts pushing at each other.
Paraphrase (German): Leibniz imagined a machine that could produce thoughts, sensations and perception, enlarged so one could walk inside.

references.name: L'Homme Machine (Man a Machine)
references.author: Julien Offray de La Mettrie
references.tldr: A scandalous Enlightenment pamphlet arguing that humans are entirely physical machines, not different in kind from animals, and that mind is a function of organised matter.
references.bach_take: Bach counts La Mettrie among the founders of the AI project: he saw humans as mathematical machines with a cybernetic motivation made of 'opposing springs'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (garbled as 'Julian of f lri' and 'L machine'): La Mettrie had the insight that humans can be understood as machines and our motivation might be cybernetic, composed of opposing springs.
Paraphrase (German): La Mettrie, a late contemporary of Leibniz, wrote 'L'homme machine' and held that the world is completely physical and man a kind of animal.

references.notes: Garbled in captions ('lri', 'lombagine'); the German transcript has 'La Mettrie' clearly.

references.name: John Locke on consciousness
references.author: John Locke
references.tldr: Locke defined consciousness as the perception of what passes in one's own mind, and tied personal identity to this continuity of awareness and memory.
references.bach_take: Bach calls this 'a pretty good idea' but notes that we actually get little awareness of what happens in our minds; the continuity of experience is stitched together after the fact.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Maybe it's the awareness of what happens in our mind. I think it's a pretty good idea that John Lochhead

references.notes: Machine subtitle writes 'John Lochhead'; resolved to John Locke from the definition given.

references.name: Immanuel Kant
references.tldr: German philosopher who tried to ground morality in reason alone: act only on rules you could will to be universal laws, regardless of culture or consequences.
references.bach_take: Mentioned only in a Q&A answer: Bach doubts that morality can be defined outside a framework of social norms that people agree on.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: This project of defining morality without societies exists longer than Kant of course.

references.name: Phenomenology (noesis, noema, epoché)
references.author: Edmund Husserl
references.tldr: Husserl argued that we never see the world itself, only appearances (phenomena). The mind turns them into meaningful objects (noema) through acts of interpretation (noesis), and philosophy should 'bracket' claims about the outside world (epoché) to study this.
references.bach_take: Bach uses Husserl to pose the problem, then offers a way out: a robot gets only bits at its interface, and a cognitive architecture can turn bits into something that looks like phenomena.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (heavily garbled subtitles): reality is not given directly; we get phenomena, the mind turns them into noema, and the process is called noesis.
Paraphrase (German): we could begin our journey with Edmund Husserl ... what we perceive of the world are appearances, phenomena; the process of turning them into ideas he calls noesis.

references.notes: 31C3 machine subtitles render noema/noesis/epoché as 'Nguema', 'Noisette', 'if hookey' and do not print Husserl's name; the German 2017 transcript names 'Edmund Husserl' explicitly.

references.name: Gottlob Frege
references.tldr: German logician whose 'Begriffsschrift' (concept script) created modern formal logic: a precise notation in which reasoning could be checked mechanically.
references.bach_take: Part of Bach's lineage of the AI project: Frege wanted a calculus for thinking.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (garbled as 'godlo frer'): Gottlob Frege had the idea of coming up with a formal language for thinking.
Paraphrase (garbled as 'frager'): Frege built a calculus in which he hoped to be able to express thoughts.

references.notes: Name garbled in auto-captions; resolved from context.

references.name: Alfred Tarski
references.tldr: Polish logician who gave the standard formal definition of truth for logical languages and put semantics on a rigorous footing.
references.bach_take: A brief stop in Bach's lineage: Tarski 'formalized logic for us' and fixed problems Aristotle did not see.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: taski formalized Logic for us
tarski who made progress and fixing the issues with logic that Aristotle didn't see yet

references.name: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: A short, austere book that tries to state exactly what can be said in language: the world is the totality of facts, language pictures facts, and what cannot be said clearly must be passed over in silence.
references.bach_take: Bach reads it as a coder's attempt to build 'a programming language for thought', pre-empting the logicist programme of AI by decades, and says philosophers misread it as being about natural language.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: It's an attempt by a guy who was basically a coder, an AI scientist, to reverse engineer the language of his own thinking.
Paraphrase: Wittgenstein had the idea of translating English into something like a programming language so philosophy could be true or false.

references.name: Philosophical Investigations
references.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: Wittgenstein's later work, which abandons the idea of one exact logical language. Meaning comes from how words are used in many overlapping 'language games'.
references.bach_take: Bach presents it as Wittgenstein's admission that the Tractatus project failed because the world is too ambiguous, the same wall symbolic AI later hit.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: In the end he wrote the book "Philosophical Investigations", where he concluded, that his project basically failed.

references.name: Cantor's set theory (power sets and infinities)
references.author: Georg Cantor
references.tldr: Cantor showed that infinite sets come in different sizes: the set of all subsets of a set is always larger than the set itself. Applied to 'the set of all sets' this produces contradictions.
references.bach_take: Bach uses it as the opening of the story of how mathematics discovered problems in its own foundations, leading to Gödel, Turing and computation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the cardinality of a set grows slower than the cardinality of the set of its subsets

references.notes: The subtitle reads 'In 1874 discovered when you looked at...' with the name dropped; resolved to Georg Cantor from date and content.

references.name: Russell's paradox
references.author: Bertrand Russell
references.tldr: Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does it contain itself? If it does, it doesn't; if it doesn't, it does. The paradox showed that naive set theory is inconsistent.
references.bach_take: A step in Bach's foundations story; he also mentions Russell's antinomy when answering a question about hierarchy in living systems.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Does the set of the sets that doesn't contain themselves contain itself? If it does, it doesn't, and if it doesn't, it does.

references.name: Hilbert's program
references.author: David Hilbert
references.tldr: Hilbert asked mathematicians to prove, by purely mechanical means, that mathematics is consistent and complete, so that every true statement could in principle be derived.
references.bach_take: Bach jokes that Hilbert was 'some kind of a community manager' who told people to fix the bug in mathematics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: So David Hilbert, who was some kind of a community manager back then, said: "Guys, fix this!

references.name: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
references.author: Kurt Gödel
references.tldr: Gödel proved that any consistent formal system rich enough to do arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. He did it by encoding statements about the system as numbers inside the system.
references.bach_take: Bach rejects the reading that Gödel shows humans exceed machines. For him Gödel 'invented the emulator' and showed that classical 'stateless' mathematics breaks, so only computational (constructive) languages can be trusted.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: some philosophers argue humans can always decide what formal systems cannot, so they are more powerful than computers; 'Gödel has done this' proof for formal systems.
as soon as we allow these kinds of loops - and we cannot really exclude these loops - then our mathematics crashes.
Paraphrase (name garbled as 'C girdle'/'could G'): Gödel 'invented the emulator' by defining a logical language on top of Peano's axioms, and found that stateless mathematics leads to contradictions.
Paraphrase: some philosophers take Gödel to mean there are proofs only humans can make; Bach notes no AI company employs people to keep such proofs out of the computer.

references.name: Peano axioms
references.author: Giuseppe Peano
references.tldr: A handful of axioms that define the natural numbers and arithmetic: there is a zero, every number has a successor, and induction holds.
references.bach_take: Bach describes them as the 'virtual computer' or CPU that Gödel used to run his proof.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (garbled as 'pianos aums'): the computer Gödel found was Peano's axioms, which define the natural numbers and arithmetic over them.

references.name: Turing machine
references.author: Alan Turing
references.tldr: An imaginary device with a tape, a read-write head and a table of rules. Despite its simplicity it can carry out any calculation that any computer can, which makes it the standard definition of computation.
references.bach_take: Bach calls it a good definition but a bad metaphor, because it leaves people imagining cogs and tape. He uses it to argue that minds are computational and in fact less than Turing machines, since real systems are finite.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: The Turing machine is a good definition, but it's a very bad metaphor
It's actually much more troubling: minds are fundamentally less than Turing machines!
Paraphrase: defines a universe-computing machine with a state vector of bits, a position and instructions, 'With this, we can define the Turing machine'.

references.name: Lambda calculus
references.author: Alonzo Church
references.tldr: A way of defining computation using nothing but functions and substitution: you replace variables in an expression with arguments, over and over. It is exactly as powerful as a Turing machine and underlies languages such as Lisp.
references.bach_take: Bach offers it as 'computation without wheels', a better intuition than the Turing machine, and jokes it should be called the 'copy and paste thingi'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: It's computation without wheels. It was invented basically at the same time as the Turing machine.
he figured out together with Alonzo Church - not together, independently but at the same time

references.name: Church-Turing thesis
references.author: Alonzo Church; Alan Turing
references.tldr: The claim that every reasonable way of defining 'effective computation' (Turing machines, lambda calculus, recursive functions, any programming language) captures the same set of computable functions.
references.bach_take: A cornerstone of every Bach lecture: because all computational languages have the same power, it does not matter which one describes mind or universe.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: all the computational approaches have the same power, although all the other ones that you are able to find in the future too, is called the Church-Turing thesis.
Paraphrase: Python, assembler, the Turing machine or the lambda calculus can all be compiled into each other; 'that's called the Church-Turing thesis'.
Paraphrase: Church and Turing discovered that all implementable representational languages have the same power.

references.name: Halting problem and undecidability
references.author: Alan Turing
references.tldr: Turing showed that no general procedure can decide, for every program, whether it will eventually stop or run forever. Some well-posed questions therefore have no computable answer.
references.bach_take: Bach lists it among the true limits of computers and argues humans cannot solve such problems either.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: For instance the question whether a Turing machine ever stops for an arbitrary program.
then we cannot know whether this proof terminates.

references.name: Post machine
references.author: Emil Post
references.tldr: A model of computation proposed by Emil Post in the same year as Turing's, built from very simple instructions on a tape of marked and unmarked boxes.
references.bach_take: Named in passing as one of many equivalent definitions of computation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: For instance the post machine, which is a variation of the Turing machine

references.name: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
references.author: Alan Turing
references.tldr: The paper that asks 'Can machines think?' and replaces the question with an imitation game, later called the Turing test: if a machine can hold a conversation indistinguishable from a human's, we should grant it intelligence. It also answers a list of objections, including one from telepathy.
references.bach_take: Bach urges everyone to read it and says it already contains most important questions and answers of AI. In 2025 he revisits Turing's ignored telepathy section as a hint that part of mind may depend on resonance with other organisms.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: When Alan Turing wrote his paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” and those of you who haven’t read it should do so.
in the 1950 paper that Alan Turing talks about the Turing test. He also discusses the possibility of telepathy

references.name: Turing's reaction-diffusion model of morphogenesis
references.author: Alan Turing
references.tldr: In 'The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis' Turing showed how two chemicals that react and spread at different rates can spontaneously form spots, stripes and other biological patterns.
references.bach_take: Bach treats it as the origin of a third, neglected tradition in AI: self-organisation, next to symbolic AI and deep learning.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the tradition of self-organization 'has been started by Turing in the 1950s' but was never followed up much.
Paraphrase: this thread of AI started with Turing's work on reaction-diffusion models that he tried to get to compute.

references.name: Chinese room argument
references.author: John Searle
references.tldr: Searle imagines a person who follows a rulebook to answer Chinese questions without understanding Chinese. He concludes that running a program is not enough for understanding; brains have special causal powers.
references.bach_take: Bach mentions the Chinese room in passing and mocks Searle's related claim that a Turing machine built from 'cats, mice and cheese' could not think, by calculating how large such a machine would be.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: John Searle said— you know, Searle is the one with the Chinese room. We’re not going to go into that
So it’s intrinsic powers of biological neurons.

references.name: Quantum consciousness (Orch-OR)
references.author: Roger Penrose; Stuart Hameroff
references.tldr: Penrose argues that human understanding is not computable and must rely on new quantum physics; with Hameroff he locates it in microtubules inside neurons.
references.bach_take: Bach rejects it: quantum processes are computable too, so the theory just 'shrouds one mystery in another'. He jokes that Penrose would explain bird flight with microtubules, but grants that Hameroff might ironically turn out right.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: he perceives kind of mechanics as mysterious and perceives consciousness as mysterious and tries to shroud one mystery in another.
If you ask Roger Penrose, he will say it's quantum mechanics. These birds have very special microtubules
Stuart Hameroff believes it's not between cells. He believes it's between microtubules. And he is a little bit alone with this.

references.name: Daniel Dennett
references.tldr: American philosopher who defended a functionalist, deflationary view of consciousness: there is no inner 'Cartesian theater' where experience happens, only many parallel processes whose results we report. He also attacked the idea of philosophical zombies.
references.bach_take: An ally. Bach quotes him on philosophy being dragged forward by other sciences, lists the 'Cartesian theater' among theories converging on his own, and in 2024 uses Dennett's 'zank' and 'zimbo' thought experiments while marking his death.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Daniel Dennett has said that philosophy of mind has come a long way during the last hundred years.
Paraphrase (garbled as 'Daniel danard'): Dennett, 'a philosopher who we lost this year', was one of the main thinkers of computational philosophy of mind and functionalism.
Dennett and Drescher's Cartesian theater

references.notes: AGI-24 transcript pairs Dennett with 'Drescher' (presumably Gary Drescher); 37C3 captions read 'how danet calls it'.

references.name: Zimbo (and 'zank')
references.author: Daniel Dennett
references.tldr: A zombie is a being that behaves as if conscious with nobody home. Dennett's 'zimbo' is a zombie with higher-order self-monitoring, so it believes and reports that it is conscious. His 'zank' is a parody: something that works exactly like a bank but supposedly lacks the essence of a bank.
references.bach_take: Bach asks whether AI models that describe themselves as conscious are zimbos, and whether we are.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: there also a question of whether we are zimbos

references.name: Philosophical zombie
references.author: David Chalmers
references.tldr: A hypothetical creature physically and behaviourally identical to a person but with no inner experience. If such a being is conceivable, the argument goes, consciousness is something over and above physical function.
references.bach_take: Bach sides with Dennett that the idea makes little sense under functionalism, but uses it to frame how hard it is to tell simulated from 'real' consciousness in language models.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (names garbled as 'David Charmers and niggle and block'): the philosophical zombies discussion was brought up by David Chalmers, Nagel and Block.

references.name: The hard problem of consciousness
references.author: David Chalmers
references.tldr: Explaining how the brain processes information is the 'easy' problem. The hard problem is why any of that processing is accompanied by subjective experience, by 'what it is like'.
references.bach_take: Bach thinks the hard problem is a cultural artefact of the 20th century: it arises because we forget that both experience and the 'physical world' we touch are representations in the mind, and because philosophers do not care how computers work.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the hard problem is caused by us existing inside biological computers 'and philosophers not actually caring about how computers work'.
this hard problem seems to be a somewhat recent problem. Most cultures don't have it.
the hard problem of consciousness doesn't seem to be an issue for him

references.name: Thomas Nagel ('What is it like to be a bat?')
references.author: Thomas Nagel
references.tldr: Nagel argued that an organism is conscious if there is 'something it is like' to be it, and that objective science cannot capture this subjective point of view.
references.bach_take: Bach uses the phrase 'what it's like' as his definition of phenomenology, parodies the argument ('what is it like to be a bird? You'll never know'), and lists Nagel among philosophers who find machine consciousness preposterous.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: they will tell you, what is it like to be a bird? You'll never know.
Paraphrase: some philosophers think machine consciousness is a preposterous idea, 'like Anil Seth and Thomas Nagel and so on and Ned Block'.

references.notes: The bat paper itself is not named; the 33C3 line is an unmistakable allusion. AGI-25 captions read 'Anel Seth ... Thomas Nagel ... Net Block'.

references.name: Access vs phenomenal consciousness
references.author: Ned Block
references.tldr: Block separated two meanings of consciousness: phenomenal (raw experience) and access (information being available for reasoning, report and action).
references.bach_take: Bach uses the terms without naming Block and defines both as kinds of memory: of the binding state and of using attention. Elsewhere Block is named as a sceptic of machine consciousness.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Phenomenal consciousness is the memory of the binding state
Access consciousness is the memory of using our attentional system.

references.notes: Block is not named in 35C3; attribution of the distinction is from background knowledge. He is named in 38C3 and AGI-25.

references.name: Qualia
references.author: C. I. Lewis (term)
references.tldr: The philosophers' word for the felt qualities of experience: the redness of red, the painfulness of pain.
references.bach_take: Bach treats qualia as perceptual features of the mind's model as seen from the perspective of the self, not as something beyond function.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: philosophers have introduced the term qualia to talk about perceptual features

references.name: Epiphenomenalism
references.tldr: The view that conscious experience is a by-product of brain activity with no causal influence on the physical world, like steam from a locomotive.
references.bach_take: Bach rejects it twice: in 2014 as an inconvenient consequence of read-only dualism, and in 2025 with the quip that an epiphenomenalist's report is not caused by their consciousness, so you need not listen.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (subtitle: 'This is called epiphenomenal, and it's a bit inconvenient'): if mind reads from but cannot write to the universe, experience is causally irrelevant.
this idea that consciousness has no causal role is called epiphenomenalism

references.name: Occasionalism
references.author: Nicolas Malebranche
references.tldr: A 17th-century answer to the mind-body problem: mind and matter never interact; God synchronises them on each occasion.
references.bach_take: Bach mentions it as a contrived escape from epiphenomenalism before proposing that mind is simply computed inside the universe.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (subtitle: 'This is called occasional ism in philosophy'): the universe would duplicate the equivalent of mental states.

references.name: Idealism
references.tldr: The family of views on which mind or experience is fundamental and the physical world derives from it.
references.bach_take: Bach says idealism and materialism are complementary: we do live in a dream, but the dreamer is a physical brain. Asked in 2024 about books claiming the universe emerges from consciousness, he replies that this explains nothing about how it works.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: So an alternative is idealism which says that there is only a mental world.
So these ideas of materialism and idealism are not in opposition.
if Consciousness is fundamental I don’t know how it actually works

references.notes: In the 38C3 Q&A a questioner cited the books 'The Matter with Things' and 'Irreducible'; Bach answered the general position without discussing the books.

references.name: Materialism / physicalism
references.tldr: The view that everything that exists is physical, and mind is something physical systems do.
references.bach_take: Bach calls it the dominant view and broadly accepts it, but prefers to say information and computation are primary and both 'mind' and 'matter' are constructions.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: matter is primary and mind emerges over functionality of matter, which is I think the dominant theory today and usually, we call it physicalism.

references.name: Functionalism
references.author: Hilary Putnam and others
references.tldr: The view that mental states are defined by what they do (their causal role), not by what they are made of, so the same mind could run on different substrates.
references.bach_take: Bach's stated position from 2018 onward. By 2025 he calls it 'computationalist functionalism' and insists it is a metaphysical stance about how we construct objects from observed behaviour, not an empirical claim that laptops can think.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And the answer that I am suggesting, is functionalism which means that indeed we exist only in a dream.
Computationalism is a theory of representation and functionalism is a theory of epistemology.

references.name: Computationalism (weak and strong)
references.tldr: Weak computationalism says minds are computer programs realised in brains. Strong computationalism (digital physics, pancomputationalism) adds that the universe itself is best described as computation that generates patterns of information.
references.bach_take: This is Bach's core thesis across the series: a new monism in which information and computation are primary. Later he sharpens it: no implementable language can do more than a finite automaton.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: but rather computationalism, which means that information and computation are primary.
strong computationalism basically no implementable language can do more than a finite automaton

references.name: Panpsychism, illusionism, mysterianism
references.tldr: Three rival responses to the hard problem: consciousness is in all matter (panpsychism); it does not really exist and only the belief in it needs explaining (illusionism); or it is real but beyond human understanding (mysterianism).
references.bach_take: Bach lists them in 2025 as the confused side of philosophy of mind, in contrast to a cluster of functional theories that converge.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: There's the position of mysterionism which says that consciousness is outside the realm of being understandable by our minds.

references.name: Franz Brentano
references.tldr: Austrian philosopher-psychologist who revived the idea of intentionality: mental states are always 'about' something. He taught Husserl and Freud.
references.bach_take: Named as a post-Enlightenment thinker who did not yet have the 'hard problem', supporting Bach's claim that it is a 20th-century confusion.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (captions: 'when you read Ga and uh Brenano'): they are post-Enlightenment and don't have this issue.

references.name: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence
references.author: Joscha Bach

references.name: Psi theory

references.name: Solomonoff induction
references.author: Ray Solomonoff
references.tldr: A mathematical ideal of learning: consider every program that could have produced your observations, weight shorter programs more heavily (Occam's razor), and predict accordingly. It is provably optimal but not computable.

references.author: Joscha Bach; Priska Herger

references.bach_take: Bach's default physics. Since only computation can be constructed, any consistent description of the universe must be computational. He calls the result a 'causally closed lookup table' whose computer we cannot inspect.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (garbled as 'Tofte'): Gerard 't Hooft, the physics Nobel laureate, wrote a book on the cellular automaton interpretation of quantum mechanics.

references.name: Conway's Game of Life
references.author: John Horton Conway

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the most famous automaton is Conway's Game of Life; it has gliders and spaceships, is Turing complete, and a continuous version with discs produces smoother moving patterns.

references.name: Simulation hypothesis
references.author: Nick Bostrom

references.name: Mandelbrot set
references.author: Benoit Mandelbrot
references.tldr: A fractal produced by repeating a one-line formula; it shows endless detail at every scale.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: imagine living inside the Mandelbrot fractal; you can predict shapes locally, but finding the formula requires stepping outside.

references.name: Genesis 1 as a theory of consciousness
references.tldr: The first chapter of the Bible tells how God creates light and darkness, separates sky and earth, makes plants and animals, and finally makes humans in his own image.
references.bach_take: Bach reads it as a 'six-stage theory' of how a mind boots: consciousness hovers over an unstructured substrate, creates contrast, a world model (earth) and sphere of ideas (heaven), then objects, agents, and finally a personal self in its own image. He thinks mistranslation turned this into a physical creation story.

Paraphrase: the Genesis story as cognitive development: first light and darkness, then separating world model from ideas, and finally creating the self in its image.

references.name: Animism
references.tldr: The widespread traditional belief that animals, plants, places and objects are inhabited by spirits. It survives in Japanese Shinto and in European fairy lore.
references.bach_take: Bach rehabilitates it as 'cyber animism': spirits are self-organising software agents running on living matter. Animism was the normal view of most cultures, and ours forgot it. He speculates that conscious AI could bridge to other 'spirits' in nature.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: it makes it very hard to translate ideas from Buddhism or from Japanese animism or from Scandinavian mythology into our own culture

references.name: Cyber animism
references.author: Joscha Bach
references.tldr: Bach's name for the view that living things are animated by self-organising software ('spirits') that can in principle run on different substrates, and that consciousness is the simplest such organising pattern.
references.bach_take: His own synthesis from 2023 onward, combining Aristotle's psyche, animist traditions, Levin's biology and computationalism.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: living things are colonised by self-organising software; evolution is a competition between software agents that only partly encode themselves in genomes.
Paraphrase: software is spirit, a causal pattern without physical identity that nevertheless moves matter; living stuff is software colonising regions of the physical universe.

references.name: Buddhism and meditation (Vipassana, jhanas, nirvana, enlightenment)
references.tldr: Buddhist practice trains attention to observe how experience and the sense of self are constructed. Vipassana is insight meditation, the jhanas are states of deep absorption, and nirvana is release from craving.
references.bach_take: Bach treats contemplatives as skilled introspectors and translates their terms into his model: enlightenment is noticing that the self is a representation; nirvana is disengaging the reward loop. He warns that meditating into bliss is hacking your reward function.

references.author: Joscha Bach
references.tldr: The idea that religions are packages of beliefs and norms installed in many minds so that large groups can coordinate. Richard Dawkins coined the related term 'virus of the mind'.
references.bach_take: In 2015 Bach calls religions mind viruses that also work as an operating system for societies beyond tribe size, and compares their family tree to that of programming languages. Later he defines a god as a self that runs across many brains.

Paraphrase (German): the genealogy of religions looks like the family tree of programming languages.

references.name: Christian mind-body dualism ('crypto-dualism')
references.tldr: The traditional Christian teaching that a person has an immaterial soul distinct from the body.
references.bach_take: Bach says the West's scepticism about AI, which he does not find in China or Japan, is rooted in the Christian idea of a metaphysical domain where souls and values really live. He calls the leftover attitude 'crypto-dualism'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And in our culture the prevalent view is what I would call crypto-dualism.

references.name: The Enlightenment
references.tldr: The 18th-century European movement that put reason, evidence and individual autonomy above religious and traditional authority.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: people have invented rationalism and enlightenment, basically to act as immunization against mind viruses.

references.name: Romanticism
references.tldr: The artistic and philosophical movement that reacted to the Enlightenment by celebrating feeling, nature, and the infinite.
references.bach_take: Bach reads Romanticism as a fight against rationalism: an attempt to keep meaning, purpose and the sacred in a universe that science had described as mere mechanism. He then explains that sense of the sacred through multilevel selection.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (garbled subtitles): as a result we got Romanticism, which is basically the fight against rationalism, to keep the sense of meaning and connection to something beyond.
